spark.summary: Calling CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() without an explicit Executor routes tasks onto ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (sized to CPU_cores - 1), where blocking I/O and nested .join() calls cause total thread starvation and self-deadlock.
spark.keyTakeaway: Always pass an isolated I/O Executor (or Java 21+ Virtual Threads) to supplyAsync(), chain dependencies with non-blocking thenComposeAsync(), and bound tails with orTimeout().
spark.byteSummary:
In Java, `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(supplier)` without a second `Executor` argument defaults to `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, which provisions only `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1` worker threads (e.g., 7 threads on an 8-core host, or just 1 thread in a 2-vCPU container).

Because `commonPool()` is designed for short, CPU-bound fork/join computations—not blocking network or database I/O—a burst of blocking HTTP calls quickly pins every worker thread. Worse, if an outer task running on `commonPool()` spawns a nested `supplyAsync()` subtask and calls `.join()` or `.get()` on it, all workers block waiting for subtasks sitting in the work queue that no free thread can execute, creating a permanent self-deadlock.

Preventing pool starvation requires two disciplines: isolate blocking I/O onto a dedicated bounded `ExecutorService` or `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`, and replace blocking `.join()` calls inside async callbacks with non-blocking `thenComposeAsync()` + `orTimeout()`.

learningJourney.title: Stage 1: Why ForkJoinPool.commonPool() Has Only (CPU - 1) Threads
learningJourney.purpose: Understand the sizing and work-stealing design of ForkJoinPool.commonPool() and why container vCPU limits shrink it further.
learningJourney.explanation: `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` sizes its parallelism to `availableProcessors() - 1` (minimum 1) so CPU-bound tasks saturate cores without context-switching overhead. Inside Kubernetes pods with `limits.cpu: 2`, `commonPool()` has literally 1 worker thread—meaning a single blocking I/O call stalls every `parallelStream()` and default `CompletableFuture` in the JVM.

sectionDiagram.title: Shared JVM-Wide ForkJoinPool.commonPool() Contention

cards.label: JVM-Wide Blast Radius
cards.detail: Every library using default supplyAsync() or parallelStream() competes for the exact same 1..7 threads.

cards.label: Container Trap
cards.detail: A 2-vCPU container gives commonPool() a parallelism of 1, turning any blocking call into a global bottleneck.

sectionDiagram.summary: Default CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() and parallelStream() share a tiny (CPU - 1) commonPool() across the entire JVM.
sectionDiagram.caption: Default CompletableFuture tasks and parallelStream() share ForkJoinPool.commonPool() sized to CPU_cores - 1.

learningJourney.title: Stage 2: Anatomy of a Nested .join() Self-Deadlock
learningJourney.purpose: Trace how an outer commonPool() task calling .join() on an inner commonPool() task deadlocks all worker threads.
learningJourney.explanation: Suppose an 8-core host (7 `commonPool()` threads) receives 7 concurrent outer tasks that each submit a nested `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()` subtask and call `subtask.join()`. All 7 workers block inside `.join()`, while the 7 subtasks sit in the `ForkJoinPool` submission queue waiting for a worker thread—deadlocking permanently without external timeouts.

sectionDiagram.title: 7 Outer Tasks Blocking on 7 Queued Subtasks in commonPool()

cards.label: ManagedBlocker Gap
cards.detail: Unlike ForkJoinTask.fork()/join() work-stealing, CompletableFuture.join() does not compensate with extra threads unless wrapped in ManagedBlocker.

cards.label: Silent Hang
cards.detail: Thread dumps show all ForkJoinPool-1-worker-* threads in WAITING at CompletableFuture.waitingGet.

sectionDiagram.summary: Calling .join() inside a commonPool() task on another commonPool() task causes permanent thread-starvation deadlock when workers fill.
sectionDiagram.caption: Outer tasks occupy all commonPool() workers calling .join() while inner subtasks wait forever in the submission queue.

learningJourney.title: Stage 3: Isolating Blocking I/O with Dedicated Executors
learningJourney.purpose: Separate blocking HTTP/DB I/O from CPU compute pools using explicit bounded ExecutorService arguments.
learningJourney.explanation: Passing an explicit `Executor` as the second argument to `supplyAsync(fn, ioExecutor)` and `*Async(..., ioExecutor)` guarantees tasks never touch `commonPool()`. Bounding the I/O pool with a finite queue (`ArrayBlockingQueue`) and `CallerRunsPolicy` or `AbortPolicy` also enforces backpressure when downstream databases slow down.

sectionDiagram.title: Bulkheading Blocking I/O onto a Dedicated Bounded Executor

cards.label: Zero Cross-Contamination
cards.detail: A slow payment gateway only saturates its dedicated I/O pool without freezing unrelated CPU pipelines.

cards.label: Avoid Unbounded Queues
cards.detail: Never use Executors.newFixedThreadPool() with an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue under bursty traffic.

sectionDiagram.summary: Passing a dedicated bounded I/O Executor to supplyAsync() isolates blocking calls from commonPool() and provides backpressure.
sectionDiagram.caption: Dedicated bounded I/O executors isolate blocking HTTP/DB calls from ForkJoinPool.commonPool() and enforce backpressure.

learningJourney.title: Stage 4: Non-Blocking Composition with thenComposeAsync()
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate nested .join() blocking by chaining dependent futures asynchronously with thenComposeAsync().
learningJourney.explanation: Instead of blocking a worker thread inside `.join()`, `thenComposeAsync(fn, executor)` registers a non-blocking callback that only schedules the dependent stage after the upstream future completes. The worker thread is released immediately back to the pool between stages, eliminating nested-wait deadlocks.

sectionDiagram.title: Replacing Blocking .join() with Non-Blocking thenComposeAsync()

cards.label: thenCompose vs thenApply
cards.detail: Use thenCompose when the callback returns a CompletableFuture; use thenApply for synchronous value transforms.

cards.label: Always Pass Executor on *Async
cards.detail: Even on *Async methods, omitting the Executor falls back to commonPool().

sectionDiagram.summary: Chaining dependent futures with thenComposeAsync(..., executor) releases worker threads between I/O stages and prevents nested deadlocks.
sectionDiagram.caption: thenComposeAsync() chains dependent async stages without parking any worker thread on .join().

learningJourney.title: Stage 5: Java 21+ Virtual Threads & Pinning Prevention
learningJourney.purpose: Scale high-concurrency blocking I/O with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() while avoiding synchronized pinning.
learningJourney.explanation: Java 21+ Virtual Threads (`Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`) mount onto carrier threads and automatically unmount during blocking socket/JDBC I/O, supporting hundreds of thousands of concurrent calls without pool starvation. To prevent carrier-thread pinning (on Java 21-23), replace `synchronized` blocks around I/O with `ReentrantLock` and bound concurrency with a `Semaphore`.

sectionDiagram.title: Unmounting Virtual Threads on Blocking I/O Without Carrier Pinning

cards.label: Never Pool Virtual Threads
cards.detail: Create a fresh virtual thread per task; use a Semaphore to bound downstream DB connections instead of a fixed pool.

cards.label: Carrier Unmounting
cards.detail: When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, its stack is parked in heap and the carrier OS thread runs other tasks.

sectionDiagram.summary: Virtual threads eliminate I/O thread starvation when paired with Semaphore concurrency caps and ReentrantLock instead of synchronized.
sectionDiagram.caption: Virtual threads unmount on blocking I/O, while Semaphores and ReentrantLock protect downstream limits and carrier threads.

learningJourney.title: Stage 6: Fan-Out Aggregation with allOf(), orTimeout() & Fallbacks
learningJourney.purpose: Coordinate parallel microservice calls safely with explicit deadlines and per-branch exception recovery.
learningJourney.explanation: Fanning out to N downstream services via `CompletableFuture.allOf(...)` requires per-future deadlines (`orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` or `completeOnTimeout(fallback, ...)`). Without timeouts, one hung downstream call blocks the entire fan-out; pairing `allOf()` with `.exceptionally()` per branch isolates partial failures and preserves sub-20ms P99 latency.

sectionDiagram.title: Deadline-Bounded CompletableFuture.allOf() with Branch Fallbacks

cards.label: Safe .join() After allOf()
cards.detail: Calling a.join() inside allOf().thenApply() never blocks because allOf() only fires once every future is done.

cards.label: Cancel Hanging Branches
cards.detail: orTimeout() completes the future with TimeoutException; pair with HTTP client timeouts to abort underlying sockets.

sectionDiagram.summary: Bounding every fan-out branch with orTimeout() and .exceptionally() before allOf() guarantees fast, partial-failure-tolerant aggregation.
sectionDiagram.caption: Per-branch orTimeout() and .exceptionally() handlers feed CompletableFuture.allOf() for non-blocking aggregation.

learningJourney.title: Stage 7: Detecting CommonPool Leaks in Production & CI
learningJourney.purpose: Catch accidental commonPool() blocking via ArchUnit rules, BlockHound/JFR, and thread-dump diagnostics.
learningJourney.explanation: Because a single missing `executor` parameter silently routes work back to `commonPool()`, teams enforce static ArchUnit rules banning 1-arg `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync`/`thenApplyAsync`, run BlockHound or JFR `jdk.ThreadPark` profiling in staging, and monitor `ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getQueuedSubmissionCount()` in production.

sectionDiagram.title: Preventing Regressions with ArchUnit, JFR & Pool Metrics

cards.label: Zero-Cost Static Ban
cards.detail: ArchUnit fails any PR that calls CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier) without an explicit Executor.

cards.label: Thread-Dump Signature
cards.detail: Look for ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-* threads blocked in CompletableFuture.waitingGet or socketRead0.

sectionDiagram.summary: ArchUnit static bans, BlockHound/JFR checks, and Micrometer queue gauges prevent commonPool() starvation regressions.
sectionDiagram.caption: ArchUnit CI rules, BlockHound profiling, and Micrometer queue gauges detect commonPool() leaks before production outages.

knowledgeChecks.question: How many worker threads does `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` provision by default inside a 2-vCPU Kubernetes container?

options.feedback: Correct. commonPool() sizes to max(1, CPU_cores - 1), so a 2-vCPU container gets just 1 worker thread.
Incorrect. commonPool() is sized for CPU-bound work, not 200 I/O threads.
Incorrect. commonPool() uses platform threads unless you explicitly pass a virtual thread executor.

options.text: 0 threads (it runs on the caller thread synchronously).
options.feedback: Incorrect. It always provisions at least 1 worker thread.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() defaults to CPU_cores - 1 (minimum 1), making 2-vCPU containers especially vulnerable to blocking I/O.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does calling `innerFuture.join()` inside an outer `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()` task (with no Executor) cause a deadlock under load?

options.feedback: Incorrect. .join() throws unchecked CompletionException, not InterruptedException.

options.text: Because outer tasks occupy all `commonPool()` worker threads waiting on inner subtasks queued in the exact same pool with no free threads left to run them.
options.feedback: Correct. Once all CPU-1 workers block in .join(), queued subtasks can never start.

options.text: Because `CompletableFuture` only allows one future per JVM.
options.feedback: Incorrect. You can create arbitrary CompletableFuture instances.
Incorrect. thenComposeAsync() is the non-blocking fix, not the cause.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: When outer tasks block all commonPool() workers via .join(), inner subtasks submitted to the same pool starve in the queue indefinitely.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which combination safely eliminates `commonPool()` starvation for blocking I/O in Java 21+?

options.text: Use `parallelStream()` to wrap every HTTP client call.
options.feedback: Incorrect. parallelStream() also runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool().

options.text: Pass `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` (or a bounded I/O `ThreadPoolExecutor`), chain with `thenComposeAsync()`, and bound with `orTimeout()`.
options.feedback: Correct. Explicit executor isolation + non-blocking chaining + timeouts eliminate both starvation and hang risks.

options.text: Remove all timeouts so slow DB queries can finish.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Missing timeouts allow hung sockets to exhaust resources.

options.text: Wrap every HTTP call in a `synchronized` block.
options.feedback: Incorrect. synchronized blocks can pin Java 21-23 virtual thread carrier threads during I/O.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Explicit I/O executor isolation (or Virtual Threads with ReentrantLock/Semaphore), thenComposeAsync(), and orTimeout() prevent pool deadlocks.

beginner.summary: Never run slow network or database calls on Java's default `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()` pool, because it only has a few shared threads and can freeze your whole app.
beginner.keyTakeaway: Pass your own dedicated thread pool (or Virtual Threads) to `supplyAsync()` and avoid calling `.join()` inside async tasks.
beginner.byteSummary:
By default, `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()` uses a small shared pool (`commonPool()`) meant for fast math, not waiting on databases or APIs.

If you pass a dedicated I/O executor and chain steps with `thenComposeAsync()`, your service stays responsive and avoids deadlocks.

intermediate.summary: Isolate blocking I/O from `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` (CPU-1 threads) using bounded executors or Virtual Threads, non-blocking `thenComposeAsync()`, and `orTimeout()`.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: Omitting the `Executor` on `supplyAsync()` or `*Async()` methods shares `commonPool()` with `parallelStream()`, risking nested `.join()` self-deadlocks.
intermediate.byteSummary:
`ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` provisions only `CPU_cores - 1` threads. Blocking I/O plus nested `.join()` calls starve all workers while subtasks wait in the queue.

Fix this by passing a dedicated bounded I/O `ExecutorService`, chaining with `thenComposeAsync(..., ioPool)`, and enforcing `orTimeout()` deadlines.

advanced.summary: Combine Java 21+ Virtual Threads (with `Semaphore` backpressure and `ReentrantLock` to avoid pinning), `allOf()` + per-branch fallbacks, and ArchUnit/JFR CI gates.
advanced.keyTakeaway: Static ArchUnit bans on 1-arg `supplyAsync()`, BlockHound/JFR I/O detection, and Micrometer `queuedSubmissions` telemetry prevent `commonPool()` regressions.
advanced.byteSummary:
At scale, `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` unmounts blocking socket/JDBC I/O from carrier threads when guarded by `Semaphore` concurrency limits and `ReentrantLock` (avoiding `synchronized` carrier pinning).

Enforce ArchUnit rules banning 1-arg `CompletableFuture.*Async` calls and monitor `commonPool().getQueuedSubmissionCount()` in production.
